messages.subject: Repeated measures error: morel levels than subjects (balanced design)
messages.subject_clean: Repeated measures error: morel levels than subjects (balanced design)
messages.body_plain:
I'm having a problem running a repeated-measures ANOVA using ezANOVA.

I have data from 18 subjects - each subject participated in 3 conditions, and data was collected in each subject/condition combination at 29 electrode sites (1566 total data points in a balanced design with no missing cells).

When I try to run the full ANOVA
>
> model = ezANOVA(data,dv=voltage,wid=subject,within=.(electrode,channel))

I get the following error:

Error in lambda > 0 : invalid comparison with complex values Error in ezANOVA_main(data = data, dv = dv, wid = wid, within = within, : The car::Anova() function used to compute results and assumption tests seems to have failed. Most commonly this is because you have too few subjects relative to the number of cells in the within-Ss design. It is possible that trying the ANOVA again with "type=1" may yield results (but definitely no assumption tests).

Things work fine though if I include fewer levels of "electrode" than I have subjects (18 or fewer), but if I add more it fails. Why is this a problem? I wouldn't think that having greater-than-n levels for a within-subjects factor would be a problem if it's a balanced fully repeated-measures design. (SPSS will compute things just fine). Using Type I SS works, but if I select this option I won't give me the sphericity corrected p-values that I need to report.

Any help will be much appreciated.

-Trevor

messages.body_plain:
I'm actually not sure what's going on mathematically to cause car::Anova() to fail. You might try contacting John Fox (author of the car package) to inquire on this.

As an aside, might I suggest that since your data is spatial in nature (eeg sampled at various points on the head), you might benefit from actually providing that spatial information to your statistics. The mgcv::gam() function. You could do something like:

    start = proc.time()[3]
    fit = gam(
  data = data
  , formula = voltage ~
            s( subject, bs = 're' )
            + condition
            + te(
                latitude
                , theta
                , bs = 'sos'
                , d = 2
                , k = 28
                , by = condition
            )
    )
    proc.time()[3] - start

Where you recode the electrode identities into their polar spatial coordinates (latitude and theta). Usually eeg data has time as a variable, in which case you'd want:

    start = proc.time()[3]
    fit = gam(
  data = data
  , formula = voltage ~
            s( subject, bs = 're' )
            + condition
            + te(
                latitude
                , theta
                , t
                , bs = c('sos','ts')
                , d = c(2,1)
                , k = c(28,10)
                , by = condition
            )
    )
    proc.time()[3] - start

Regardless, you could then obtain predictions for either using ezPredict. I happen to be working on code to automate the process of visualizing the resulting predictions; I'll post a link in the next few days ...

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

messages.subject: within_covariates or between_covariates
messages.body_plain:
I am running ezANOVA with a complex factorial design and would like to add a covariate to my analysis. I'm unsure whether it should be a within_covariate or a between_covariate.

Here's my ezANOVA call without the covariate:

ezANOVA( data=D, wid=.(subjid), dv=.(accuracy), within=.(task,format), between=.(experiment,training) )

experiment refers to which experiment the subject comes from; it has two levels.

training refers to training condition; there are 3 levels.

task refers to one of three tasks performed, and format refers to the data format used while performing the task, which could be graph, table, or text.

For each combination of task and format, each subject has an accuracy score, which is a percentage calculated over 16 trials.

The covariate is called "influence". It ranges from -1.0 to 1.0 and also has one value for each subject for each combination of task and format.

So, "influence" should be a between_covariate or a within_covariate?

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
messages.body_plain:
And the ancova version would be:

my_aov = aov(
    data = D

    , formula = accuracy ~ experiment*training*task*format+influence+Error(subjid/(task*format+influence))
)
summary(my_aov)

Remember though: the assumptions of ancova are that the covariate doesn't interact with the other predictors (as I mentioned before) and also that the covariate isn't related to the other predictors. To evaluate the latter assumption, use ezANOVA with influence as the dv:

ezANOVA( data=D, dv=.(influence), wid=.(subjid), within=.(task,format), between=.(experiment,training) )

If you get any "significant" effects, you're violating an assumption of ancova. Note that some feel that a more lenient alpha should be used when doing assumption tests as you don't want to feel that your data are telling you that the assumption is OK simply because you have low power to detect the assumption violation.

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for all the advice! It's really beyond the call of duty.

I know that "influence" is indeed correlated with the predictors - in fact, if it weren't, this whole line of thought would probably be fruitless. What I want to do is find evidence that influence mediates the effects of the predictors on accuracy, and obviously that could only be true if it's correlated with the predictors. So ... I need an analysis which allows such a correlation. Ideally, it should be closely related to the analysis that I do WITHOUT influence included, so that the results can be meaningfully compared. It sounds like you're saying ANCOVA is not what I need because it doesn't allow said correlation. So ... what is, if anything? Suggestions?

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
messages.body_plain:
There is some controversy about this, and indeed it's been discussed on this list in the past. When ANCOVA was developed, its purpose was to enhance power by removing variance associated with the covariate. Its more typical use, however, has been to "control for" the covariate, whatever that means. It's easy to simulate (https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/3122329) to show that when ancova is used in this manner, the false-positive rate increases, which I'd consider very concerning. I'm not sure what the proper approach to the problem of inference amidst correlated predictors is though. Possibly path analysis? I've been learning Bayesian modelling lately and while I haven't actually implemented this, I think it should be pretty straightforward to include the correlations amongst the predictors as estimated parameters at least, which I believe should yield more inferentially valid estimates of the predictors' influence on the predicted variable. I think, though, sou'd still have to do something extra with the posterior samples to evaluate the predictors' independent influence.

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
